title: KV Cache Quantization: How FP8 and INT4 Compression Fit Million-Token Context Windows into High-Bandwidth Memory
summary: During autoregressive LLM inference, serving long context sequences is severely memory-bound. While model weights remain static, the Key-Value (KV) cache grows linearly with sequence length and batch size, rapidly consuming tens of gigabytes of GPU High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM). Once HBM fills up, serving engines must throttle concurrency and reject incoming requests. KV cache quantization compresses cached attention tensors from 16-bit floats to FP8 or INT4 representations on-the-fly. This cuts memory footprint by 50% to 75%, doubling maximum serving batch sizes while maintaining perplexity and retrieval accuracy.
analogyTitle: The Real-Life Analogy: The Stenographer's Shorthand Notepad vs. Full Audio Recordings
analogy:
Imagine a courtroom trial that lasts for three continuous months.

Under Full Precision FP16 KV Caching (High-Definition Audio Tapes), the court stenographer records every single witness testimony on uncompressed reel-to-reel magnetic audio tapes. By day 20, the courtroom is completely filled with thousands of tape reels stacked to the ceiling. The judge cannot seat jurors or lawyers (GPU out-of-memory), and reviewing testimony requires hauling tons of tape boxes across the room (memory bandwidth saturation).

Under KV Cache Quantization (Professional Shorthand Symbols), the stenographer uses compact standardized shorthand symbols (INT4/FP8). A 20-minute speech fits on a single index card. The courtroom filing cabinet takes up 75% less physical space, allowing the court to run four trials simultaneously in the same room without ever running out of shelf space.

sections.heading: 1. The KV Cache Memory Explosion at Scale
sections.content:
For an autoregressive transformer generating tokens, attention keys and values from previous tokens must be retained in memory to avoid quadratic recomputation.

The memory footprint of the KV cache for a model with $L$ layers, hidden dimension $d$, batch size $b$, and sequence length $s$ is governed by:

$$\text{Memory}_{\text{KV}} = 2 \times 2 \times b \times s \times L \times d \quad \text{bytes (in FP16)}$$

For a 70B parameter model ($L = 80, d = 8192$) serving a batch size of 16 at a sequence length of $32\text{K}$ tokens, the KV cache alone consumes:

$$\text{Memory}_{\text{KV}} = 4 \times 16 \times 32768 \times 80 \times 8192 \approx 1.37 \text{ Terabytes of VRAM}$$

Even distributed across an 8x H100 GPU cluster (640 GB total HBM), the KV cache vastly exceeds available memory. Compressing KV states is non-negotiable for production long-context inference.

sections.heading: 2. Inside KV Quantization: Per-Channel vs. Per-Token Scaling
sections.content:
Quantizing KV cache differs fundamentally from static weight quantization because keys and values are generated dynamically at runtime:

• Asymmetric Outliers in Keys vs. Values:
Empirical analysis reveals that Key tensors have pronounced channel-specific outlier magnitudes, whereas Value tensors are more uniformly distributed. Applying naive per-tensor INT8 quantization distorts critical attention score distributions.

• Per-Channel Key Quantization:
Modern serving engines (such as vLLM and TensorRT-LLM) apply per-channel scaling factors for keys, preserving the directional precision of attention queries:

$$K_{\text{quant}} = \text{clamp}\left(\text{round}\left(\frac{K}{\mathbf{s}_c}\right), -V_{\text{max}}, V_{\text{max}}\right)$$

• FP8 KV Caching (E4M3 and E5M2):
NVIDIA Hopper architecture allows direct matrix multiplication between FP16 Queries and FP8 Keys using Tensor Cores without upfront dequantization. Keys and values are cast to FP8 upon generation and written directly to memory buffers, cutting memory bus transactions by 50%.

sections.heading: 3. Production Benchmarks: Throughput and Retrieval Fidelity
sections.content:
Deploying KV cache quantization delivers direct operational multipliers in production clusters:

• 2x to 3x Concurrency Expansion: Slashing the KV cache footprint from 16 bits to 4 or 8 bits frees hundreds of gigabytes of HBM, allowing serving engines to increase maximum concurrent requests without running out of memory.
• Needle-in-a-Haystack Verification: On retrieval benchmarks like 'Needle In A Haystack' across 128K context windows, FP8 KV caching matches FP16 retrieval accuracy with 99.8% fidelity, while INT4 quantization with group-wise scaling retains full reasoning capability.
• Lower Time-To-First-Token (TTFT): Reduced memory traffic during attention computation accelerates memory-bound decode kernels, lowering latency for all connected users.

takeaway: The KV cache is the primary barrier to scaling context length and concurrency in production LLM inference. Compressing cached attention keys and values to FP8 or INT4 using per-channel scaling factors slashes High-Bandwidth Memory consumption by up to 75%, doubling server throughput without compromising retrieval accuracy.
